prompt: Where is the three-bit Ethernet CoS/PCP marking carried?
options: In the priority field of an IEEE 802.1Q tag
In the final three bits of an IPv4 source address
In the complete eight-bit IPv6 Traffic Class field
In the destination port of a UDP transport header
explanation: The 802.1Q priority code point has three bits. Untagged Ethernet has no PCP field, but an enclosed IP packet can still carry DSCP.

whyWrong.1: Source addresses identify endpoints; their final bits are not a QoS field.
whyWrong.2: IPv6 Traffic Class contains DSCP and ECN, not an Ethernet PCP tag.
whyWrong.3: A UDP port may be a classification criterion, but it is not a CoS marking.

prompt: On classic IOS LLQ, why is a rate allowance associated with a priority class during congestion?
options: To hold unused priority capacity idle until more voice arrives.
To bound priority consumption so other classes can receive service.
To set the same maximum rate for all nonpriority classes.
To delay excess priority packets in the congestion-time policer.
explanation: The congestion-time policer constrains the priority class's use of a busy link. Unused capacity remains available; the policy does not change link duplex.

whyWrong.0: Unused capacity can be used by other eligible traffic.
whyWrong.2: Other classes retain their own scheduling treatment.
whyWrong.3: The policer applies its configured excess action rather than creating a shaping queue.

prompt: What is the main purpose of QoS when several applications compete for a busy link?
options: Increase the physical capacity of the contracted circuit.
Remove the propagation delay between the two sites.
Allocate available forwarding service according to the traffic policy.
Reserve the same treatment across every independent provider.
explanation: QoS controls treatment of competing traffic using the available resources. End-to-end results still depend on the path, capacity and policies at other hops.

whyWrong.0: QoS allocates existing service; it does not increase the circuit capacity.
whyWrong.1: Propagation depends on the path and medium, not queue policy.
whyWrong.3: A local policy does not configure every other administrative domain.

prompt: Which action is marking rather than classification?
options: Checking whether an IP packet belongs to the managed-phone subnet.
Writing AF21 into the packet’s DSCP field.
Comparing a packet’s UDP destination with a voice-service port.
Matching a packet against a supported application signature.
explanation: Marking changes a packet field. Classification decides which category matches; a separate policy determines what to do with that category.

whyWrong.0: That test identifies a traffic category.
whyWrong.2: That compares a field against a classification criterion.
whyWrong.3: That identifies the application for classification.

prompt: Which two statements accurately compare policing and shaping? Choose two.
options: A shaper guarantees delivery by allowing an unlimited queue
A policer can remark excess traffic instead of discarding it
A policer lowers the interface's negotiated physical speed
A shaper can buffer excess traffic and add waiting time
A shaper cannot transmit a short burst above its average rate
explanation: Policing applies the configured action after metering; shaping controls departure timing with a buffer. Both can allow bursts, and a finite shaping queue can overflow.

whyWrong.0: Real buffers are finite; sustained excess demand can cause loss.
whyWrong.2: A policy rate is independent of the negotiated physical rate.
whyWrong.4: Burst allowances and measurement intervals matter; the configured average is not a limit on every instantaneous interval.

exhibit.title: Representative policer excerpt
exhibit.text:
police cir 1000000
  conform-action transmit
  exceed-action set-dscp-transmit af13
exceeded 1750 packets; actions: set-dscp-transmit

prompt: What happens to the 1,750 packets counted as exceeding this policer?
options: They wait until the policer's dedicated shaping queue drains
They are discarded because all exceed actions mean drop
They receive EF so they can bypass downstream congestion
They are transmitted with AF13 instead of their earlier mark
explanation: The explicit exceed action remarks and transmits. Downstream discard behavior depends on the downstream policy; AF13 does not force immediate loss.

whyWrong.0: This action does not create a shaping queue.
whyWrong.1: The configured action is set-dscp-transmit, not drop.
whyWrong.2: The action names AF13, which is DSCP 14, not EF.

prompt: In a supporting IOS CBWFQ policy, what does `bandwidth 512` mean for DATA?
options: A minimum 512 kb/s share during congestion, with excess capacity usable
A permanent 512 kb/s ceiling, with all additional packets discarded
A 512-byte queue limit, with later arriving packets tail-dropped
A 512 kb/s physical link speed, negotiated with the neighboring device
explanation: The bandwidth command provides a minimum class share during congestion. It is not a policer or a physical interface speed command.

whyWrong.1: A ceiling requires a rate-limiting action such as policing or shaping.
whyWrong.2: The argument here is kilobits per second, not queue bytes.
whyWrong.3: Physical speed is separate from class scheduling.

exhibit.title: Representative classic IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Class-map: VOICE
  Match: dscp ef (46)
  Priority: 128 (kbps), burst bytes 3200
  b/w exceed drops: 400

prompt: During congestion, this classic IOS LLQ counter increases by 400. What does it identify?
options: The physical interface has dropped to a speed of 128 kb/s
The voice classifier failed to match the arriving packets
The priority class exceeded its permitted rate/burst allowance
The DATA class was capped at its minimum bandwidth
explanation: The bandwidth-exceed counter belongs to the priority class's congestion-time policer. It identifies that action, not a link-speed change.

whyWrong.0: Priority policy changes service, not the Ethernet physical speed.
whyWrong.1: A class-specific policer drop occurs after traffic has been assigned to the class.
whyWrong.3: A bandwidth minimum for another class does not explain this counter.

prompt: Which interpretation of AF32 is correct?
options: DSCP 32; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 28; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 26; AF class 2 with drop precedence 3
DSCP 46; the recommended Expedited Forwarding code
explanation: AFxy uses 8x + 2y: 8×3 + 2×2 = 28. The digits identify the AF class and drop precedence, not a decimal DSCP written without conversion.

whyWrong.0: The letters and two digits are a symbolic name, not decimal 32.
whyWrong.2: AF32 uses x=3, y=2. DSCP 26 is AF31.
whyWrong.3: EF is 46; AF32 is a different codepoint.

prompt: A capture confirms that many TCP flows reduce sending together after a full FIFO queue drops a burst. Which mechanism is intended to spread earlier congestion signals across flows?
options: Strict priority for every class on the output interface
Changing all packets to the same AF drop precedence
Random early detection before the queue is completely full
Increasing each endpoint's advertised Ethernet link speed
explanation: RED/WRED can act probabilistically before a queue fills, reducing the chance that many responsive flows react to one large loss event. It does not guarantee steady utilization.

whyWrong.0: Giving everything strict priority does not distinguish traffic or provide early congestion signals.
whyWrong.1: A shared marking alone does not create early queue management.
whyWrong.3: Endpoint link speed does not remove this bottleneck's finite capacity.

prompt: Ordinary users can set DSCP on their PCs. The policy reserves preferred treatment for verified managed-phone traffic. Where should the network first validate those markings?
options: At the destination, after the traffic has already crossed the managed queues.
At the ingress boundary, before received marks select preferred treatment.
At the WAN exit only, while every earlier switch accepts endpoint markings.
At the endpoint itself, treating its self-selected value as authorization.
explanation: Validation belongs at a boundary with reliable traffic information before untrusted markings influence preferred service. A managed phone can be part of that design, but its presence alone is not authentication.

whyWrong.0: Validation after the managed queues cannot protect resources already consumed.
whyWrong.2: Earlier switches would still accept untrusted marks before the proposed WAN-only check.
whyWrong.3: The premise says users control their marks; a self-selected value is not authorization for preferred service.

prompt: A classifier requires both: source belongs to the managed-phone subnet AND DSCP is EF. A PC outside that subnet sends an EF-marked packet. How is it evaluated?
options: It matches because the EF criterion is sufficient for this rule.
It matches because source membership is checked only after queue selection.
It fails because both criteria are required and source membership fails.
It fails because the policy compares the criteria as an OR expression.
explanation: An AND rule requires both criteria. The source criterion fails even though the DSCP criterion succeeds. A PC is capable of marking EF.

whyWrong.0: That would apply OR logic to the stated AND rule.
whyWrong.1: Both stated match conditions belong to classification.
whyWrong.3: With OR, the true EF criterion would be sufficient; the configured rule is AND.

prompt: A 1,500-byte packet is serialized onto a 1 Mb/s link. Ignoring all additional framing overhead, how long does serialization take?
options: 1.5 ms
8 ms
150 ms
12 ms
explanation: 1,500 bytes × 8 = 12,000 bits; divided by 1,000,000 bits/s gives 0.012 s, or 12 ms.

whyWrong.0: This treats bytes as though they were bits.
whyWrong.1: Eight is the bits-per-byte conversion, not the resulting time.
whyWrong.2: 150 ms is a voice design guideline, not this size/rate calculation.

prompt: Two voice paths have the same average one-way delay. One varies between 20 and 100 ms while the other stays near 60 ms. Which difference matters to a playout buffer?
options: The first path has higher physical bandwidth because its minimum is lower.
The second path has higher loss because its packets share similar delay.
The first path must have lower serialization delay on every hop.
The first path has greater delay variation despite the equal average.
explanation: Jitter concerns variation, not just average delay. A playout buffer must accommodate arriving packets with different delays; averages alone hide that variation.

whyWrong.0: Delay samples do not establish physical link capacity.
whyWrong.1: Stable delay does not establish packet loss.
whyWrong.2: End-to-end delay variation does not identify a particular delay component.

prompt: Two policies see the same short excess burst after their token allowance is exhausted. One remarks and transmits it; the other has room to buffer it until transmission is allowed. Which outcome matches those actions?
options: The policer forwards with a changed mark; the shaper adds waiting time.
Both hold the excess packets until a dedicated policing queue empties.
Both discard the burst because a rate limit always means drop.
The shaper changes physical link speed; the policer reserves bandwidth.
explanation: Read the configured action rather than inferring that every rate limit drops. The shaper has finite space and may drop later if sustained demand fills it.

whyWrong.1: A policer does not create a waiting queue for excess traffic.
whyWrong.2: The specified actions are remark/transmit and buffer, not immediate drop.
whyWrong.3: Shaping controls departures, while policing applies the metered action.

exhibit.title: Observed attachment
exhibit.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1
 Service-policy input: MARK-IN
  Class-map: DEFAULT-IP
   Match: dscp default (0)

prompt: PC-A requests enter Gi0/0 and leave Gi0/1. MARK-IN is applied input on Gi0/1. Its counters increase while a ping succeeds. What should be checked before declaring requests correctly marked?
options: Inspect the request headers and move the policy to their intended ingress.
Raise the marking policy’s rate while leaving its attachment on Gi0/1.
Accept the aggregate match count as verification for both packet directions.
Replace the mark with EF while keeping the Gi0/1 input attachment.
explanation: Replies can enter Gi0/1 and increment counters even though requests enter Gi0/0. Inspect request headers and the relevant attachment; connectivity alone does not prove marking.

whyWrong.1: A rate change does not move the attachment to the requests’ Gi0/0 ingress.
whyWrong.2: Replies can increment the counter without requests encountering this policy.
whyWrong.3: A different marking action at the wrong ingress still misses the requests.

exhibit.title: Authored correlated observations
exhibit.text:
Local router: verified voice classification; priority allowance not exceeded.
Local voice-drop counter unchanged during the complaint.
Capture before/after downstream switch: the same voice stream retains EF.
Downstream shared egress queue: depth rises and drops increase during the complaint.
The downstream class mapping and scheduler have not yet been inspected.

prompt: What should be checked next to explain the voice impairment while preserving correctly classified local traffic?
options: Increase the local priority allowance because no local drops prove downstream congestion.
Set every local packet to EF so all flows use the same downstream service.
Inspect the downstream queue policy, competing demand and voice treatment during impairment.
Disable local marking because unchanged EF values prove it is unnecessary.
explanation: A preserved mark does not guarantee a particular per-hop service. Correlate the downstream queue’s behavior and class mapping with the impairment before choosing a bounded correction.

whyWrong.0: No local drops do not establish the cause or required policy on the downstream device.
whyWrong.1: That discards traffic differentiation without establishing the downstream classification or bottleneck.
whyWrong.3: The mark is preserved but its downstream treatment remains unverified.
